--- title: "Interpreting patterns, and their limits" description: "Three questions to ask of any unsupervised result: does it replicate, does it correspond to anything you did not use, and is it a group or a cut through a gradient." order: 6 categories: [unsupervised, interpretation] --- ## Why this matters You have run the analysis. There are two clusters, or three, and the ordination looks like something. Now somebody has to decide what goes in the paper. Supervised work has an answer to this: hold data out, predict it, report the error. Unsupervised work has no held-out truth to predict, so the question "is this real?" has no single number. It has three questions instead, and this page asks all three of the result from [the clustering page](clustering.qmd). ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() community <- load_coastal_community() composition <- recipe(~ ., data = dplyr::select(community, starts_with("tax"))) |> step_log(all_numeric_predictors(), offset = 1) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |> prep() |> bake(new_data = NULL) |> as.matrix() stations <- community |> inner_join(dplyr::select(survey, station_id, depth_m, substrate), by = "station_id") |> mutate(bottom = if_else(substrate %in% c("rock", "gravel"), "hard", "soft")) set.seed(11) reference <- kmeans(composition, centers = 2, nstart = 50, iter.max = 100)$cluster ``` ::: ## Question one: does it replicate? Resample the stations, cluster the resample, and ask whether you get the same partition back. The mechanics are the bootstrap from [§7](../07-validation/uncertainty-and-stability.qmd): draw 800 stations with replacement, cluster them, then assign *all* the original stations to whichever bootstrap centre is nearest and compare that against the reference partition with the adjusted Rand index. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} assign_to_nearest <- function(centres, points) { apply(points, 1, \(row) which.min(colSums((t(centres) - row)^2))) } set.seed(12) replicates <- map_dfr(1:60, \(replicate) { drawn <- sample(nrow(composition), replace = TRUE) centres <- kmeans(composition[drawn, ], centers = 2, nstart = 25, iter.max = 100)$centers relabelled <- assign_to_nearest(centres, composition) tibble(replicate = replicate, agreement = adjustedRandIndex(relabelled, reference), matches_substrate = adjustedRandIndex(relabelled, stations$bottom), depth_correlation = abs(cor(relabelled, stations$depth_m))) }) summarise(replicates, mean = mean(agreement), median = median(agreement), min = min(agreement)) |> mutate(across(everything(), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| mean| median| min| |-----:|------:|-----:| | 0.881| 0.986| 0.095|
::: ::: A mean agreement of 0.881 with the full-data partition sounds like a stable result with a bit of noise on it. The median is 0.986 and the minimum is 0.095, which should already give you pause. Look at the distribution. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(replicates, aes(agreement)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, boundary = 0, fill = ml_palette[["blue"]], colour = "white") + geom_vline(xintercept = mean(replicates$agreement), linetype = "dashed", colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], linewidth = 0.7) + annotate("text", x = mean(replicates$agreement) - 0.02, y = 40, hjust = 1, label = "mean", colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], size = 3.4) + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) + labs(x = "adjusted Rand index against the full-data partition", y = "bootstrap replicates", subtitle = "60 bootstrap clusterings at k = 2") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Agreement between 60 bootstrap clusterings and the full-data partition. There is no middle: 53 replicates reproduce the substrate split almost exactly, 7 return a completely different partition, and nothing lands in between. The mean of 0.881 describes no replicate that actually happened.](interpreting-patterns_files/figure-html/fig-bootstrap-1.png){#fig-bootstrap fig-alt='Histogram of adjusted Rand index over 60 bootstrap replicates, from 0 to 1. Seven replicates form two short bars between 0.05 and 0.15 at the far left, reaching heights of 2 and 5. Fifty-three form bars between 0.90 and 1.00 at the far right, four in the first and forty-nine in the second. The entire range between 0.15 and 0.90 is empty. A dashed vertical line marking the mean at 0.881 stands in that empty gap, immediately left of the right-hand bars.' width=1300} ::: ::: The result is bimodal. Most of the time the bootstrap recovers the partition we started with; some of the time it returns something with almost nothing in common with it. An average over those two outcomes is a number that never occurred. What are the nine? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} replicates |> mutate(outcome = if_else(agreement > 0.5, "same as full data", "something else")) |> summarise(replicates = n(), `agreement with substrate` = round(mean(matches_substrate), 3), `|correlation with depth|` = round(mean(depth_correlation), 3), .by = outcome) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|outcome | replicates| agreement with substrate| |correlation with depth|| |:-----------------|----------:|------------------------:|----------------------------------:| |same as full data | 53| 0.909| 0.228| |something else | 7| 0.100| 0.759|
::: ::: They are the depth split. The 53 majority replicates recover the hard/soft substrate boundary, agreeing with it at 0.909 and barely correlated with depth; the 7 minority replicates cut the survey by depth instead, correlating 0.76 with it. Both are genuine optima of the same objective on slightly different samples, and this dataset simply contains two competing two-cluster answers of similar quality. ::: {.callout-important} Report the distribution, not its average. A bimodal stability result is not a noisy version of one answer — it is two answers, and knowing that is far more useful than a mean. Had we reported 0.881 and moved on, we would have described the data as having one stable two-cluster structure, which is false. ::: ## Question two: is it a group, or a cut through a gradient? Now the harder one, because stability does not answer it. Take only the soft-bottom stations — one substrate, no boundary left to find — and cluster them into two. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} soft <- stations$bottom == "soft" soft_composition <- composition[soft, ] set.seed(13) soft_reference <- kmeans(soft_composition, centers = 2, nstart = 50, iter.max = 100)$cluster set.seed(14) soft_agreement <- map_dbl(1:60, \(replicate) { drawn <- sample(nrow(soft_composition), replace = TRUE) centres <- kmeans(soft_composition[drawn, ], centers = 2, nstart = 25, iter.max = 100)$centers adjustedRandIndex(assign_to_nearest(centres, soft_composition), soft_reference) }) c(mean = mean(soft_agreement), min = min(soft_agreement), `median depth of cluster 1` = median(stations$depth_m[soft][soft_reference == 1]), `median depth of cluster 2` = median(stations$depth_m[soft][soft_reference == 2])) |> round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> mean min median depth of cluster 1 #> 0.89 0.71 123.70 #> median depth of cluster 2 #> 59.90 ``` ::: ::: This partition is **more** stable than the substrate one: mean agreement 0.890 and never below 0.71, against a bimodal 0.881 that reached 0.095 at its worst. It splits the soft bottom into a shallow group at a median of 60 m and a deep group at a median of 124 m. It would pass any stability check you cared to apply, and a paper describing "two distinct soft-sediment assemblages" would look well supported. It corresponds to nothing. We know, because we wrote the generator: every taxon was given a depth optimum, and the optima were **spread evenly** from 20 m to 160 m. There are no soft-sediment assemblages in this data. There is one continuous turnover, and k-means cut it in half, in the same place every time — which is why the cut is stable. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} soft_taxa <- load_coastal_community_taxa() |> filter(group == "soft-substrate") |> arrange(depth_optimum_m) # The two clusters overlap in depth, so there is no sharp edge to draw. This is the # midpoint between their median depths — the cut the partition amounts to. boundary <- mean(tapply(stations$depth_m[soft], soft_reference, median)) community |> inner_join(dplyr::select(stations, station_id, depth_m, bottom), by = "station_id") |> filter(bottom == "soft") |> pivot_longer(all_of(soft_taxa$taxon), names_to = "taxon", values_to = "count") |> left_join(soft_taxa, by = "taxon") |> mutate(taxon = fct_reorder(taxon, depth_optimum_m)) |> ggplot(aes(depth_m, count, colour = depth_optimum_m, group = taxon)) + geom_vline(xintercept = boundary, linetype = "dashed", colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) + geom_smooth(se = FALSE, method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, span = 0.6, linewidth = 0.9) + scale_colour_viridis_c(name = "true depth optimum (m)") + labs(x = "depth (m)", y = "smoothed mean count", subtitle = "Soft-substrate taxa along the depth gradient") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Eight soft-substrate taxa across the depth range, each smoothed over the soft-bottom stations. The peaks slide steadily along the axis and neighbouring curves overlap heavily; there is no depth at which one set of taxa hands over to another. The dashed line is the midpoint between the two clusters' median depths — the cut the partition amounts to.](interpreting-patterns_files/figure-html/fig-continuum-1.png){#fig-continuum fig-alt='Line chart of smoothed mean count against depth from 0 to 180 metres, one line per taxon for eight soft-substrate taxa, coloured by true depth optimum from dark for shallow to yellow for deep. The peaks are staggered across the whole range, the darkest peaking near 20 metres and the palest near 155 metres, with each curve rising and falling over roughly 100 metres so that neighbouring curves overlap heavily and several taxa are abundant at every depth. No gap or step appears anywhere along the axis. A dashed vertical line near 92 metres marks the midpoint between the two clusters.' width=1500} ::: ::: This is the single most important picture in the section. A gradient and a set of groups look identical once you have turned them into cluster labels, and no amount of resampling will tell them apart, because a stable algorithm cuts a stable gradient in a stable place. ## Question three: does it correspond to anything you did not use? The only thing that separated the two cases was information from outside the clustering. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} depth_band <- cut(stations$depth_m, breaks = quantile(stations$depth_m, c(0, 1/3, 2/3, 1)), include.lowest = TRUE) tibble(`clustering of` = c("all stations, k = 2", "soft stations only, k = 2"), `vs substrate` = c(adjustedRandIndex(reference, stations$bottom), adjustedRandIndex(soft_reference, stations$bottom[soft])), `vs depth tertile` = c(adjustedRandIndex(reference, depth_band), adjustedRandIndex(soft_reference, depth_band[soft]))) |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|clustering of | vs substrate| vs depth tertile| |:-------------------------|------------:|----------------:| |all stations, k = 2 | 0.92| 0.02| |soft stations only, k = 2 | 0.00| 0.40|
::: ::: The whole-survey clustering matches substrate at 0.920 and depth tertiles at 0.020: it has found a categorical variable it was never shown. The soft-only clustering matches substrate at 0.000, which it must, since every station in it has the same substrate — and matches depth tertiles at 0.40, which is what cutting a continuous variable into classes and then comparing against arbitrary classes of the same variable always gives. That is the asymmetry to hold on to. Agreement with a **categorical** external variable is evidence of groups. Agreement with a **continuous** one, binned for the comparison, is evidence only of a gradient — and a gradient is a finding too, just not the one the word "cluster" implies. ::: {.callout-warning} Whatever you validate against must be information the clustering did not have. Cluster a community matrix and check against substrate, salinity, season, a seabed map — anything measured separately. Clustering the environment *and* the community together and then noting that the clusters differ environmentally proves nothing at all. ::: ## What you can write down From everything on this page, the defensible claims about this survey are: - Composition separates into **hard-bottom and soft-bottom** assemblages, recovered without substrate information, matching the seabed classification at an adjusted Rand index of 0.920, and reproduced in 53 of 60 bootstrap replicates. - Within each of those, composition **turns over continuously with depth**, with no detectable boundary; a two-cluster split of the soft bottom is stable but describes a cut at about 92 m rather than two assemblages. - The remaining 7 bootstrap replicates preferred the depth split, so the substrate boundary is the stronger of two competing structures rather than the only one. And the claims that are not available: - Any count of "assemblages" on this shelf beyond the two substrate groups. - Any statement that a principal component *is* the depth gradient — it is at [about 45° to both axes](principal-component-analysis.qmd). - Any interpretation of distance or cluster size in [the UMAP picture](dimensionality-reduction.qmd). ::: {.callout-note} ## What unsupervised methods are actually for Nothing here says the analysis was a waste. Clustering found a real boundary from counts alone, the ordination separated a boundary from a gradient at a glance, and two components predicted station depth to 21 m. Unsupervised methods are excellent at generating hypotheses and at compressing data you cannot otherwise look at. They are weak at confirming anything, because there is nothing held out to confirm against. Use them to decide what to measure next, and reach for [§7's machinery](../07-validation/index.qmd) when something needs testing. ::: ## Where this leaves the course [§9](../09-neural-networks/index.qmd) takes up representation learning, where an autoencoder does what PCA does without the linearity — and inherits every interpretation problem on this page along with it. [§10](../10-interpretation/index.qmd) takes up the rest. The bimodal bootstrap here is a small version of a general problem: a single number from a single run, reported without its distribution, is the most common way that a plausible result becomes a wrong one. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Key points - Ask three questions of any unsupervised result: does it **replicate**, is it a **group or a cut**, and does it match something **external**. - Report the whole stability distribution. Ours was bimodal — 53 replicates found the substrate split, 7 found a depth split — and its mean of 0.881 described neither. - **Stability is necessary, not sufficient.** The soft-bottom depth split was the most stable result on the page and corresponds to nothing: a stable algorithm cuts a stable gradient in a stable place. - External validation is the strongest evidence available, and only if the variable was withheld from the clustering. Matching a **categorical** variable is evidence of groups; matching a **binned continuous** one is not. - Write down the gradient as a finding. "Composition turns over continuously with depth" is a result, and a more honest one than a cluster count. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Run the bootstrap at $k = 3$ instead of 2. Is the distribution bimodal there too, and which structures are competing? 2. Cluster the soft-bottom stations into two using only the three taxa that respond to nothing (`tax22`–`tax24`). How stable is *that* partition, and what does its stability tell you?
